traits: Nighttime scurrying in the attic or ceiling void
Sleek, dark gray-brown, tail longer than the body
Travels power lines, fences, and palm fronds like a tightrope
Hollowed-out citrus still on the tree

look_alikes.difference: Roof rats are found up high (attic, roofline, trees) with a tail longer than the body; Norway rats burrow at ground level and have a shorter, thicker tail.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the droppings' size and shape, plus a wide shot of where the activity is (attic vs. ground).

copy.what_it_means: Florida's aerialist — it runs fences and branches like a tightrope walker and enters at roofline, not floor level. Attic noise plus chewed wires is worth an inspection; sealing entry points (exclusion) is the standard approach once the entries are found.
copy.fact: It runs fences and branches like a tightrope walker and enters buildings at roofline, not floor level.
copy.blurb: Attic noise + chewed wires is worth an inspection. Exclusion (sealing entry points) is the standard approach, done after the entries are located.

tech_notes: Confirm tail-longer-than-body + roofline entry signs. Full exclusion walk (roof returns, AC chase, garage corners); quote trapping + exclusion after inspection.

Heavier build than a roof rat, tail shorter than the body
Greasy rub marks along baseboards and pipes
Ground-floor and burrow specialist, rarely climbs high

copy.what_it_means: Where roof rats take the high road, Norway rats dig in at the foundation. A burrow plus droppings suggests an established population; an inspection confirms the extent, then trapping paired with sealing entry points, in that order.
copy.fact: Ground-floor specialist — where roof rats take the high road, Norway rats dig in at the foundation.
copy.blurb: Burrow + droppings suggest an established population. An inspection confirms it, then trapping plus entry sealing, in that order.

traits: Rice-grain-sized droppings in drawers and under sinks
Gnawed corners on food packaging
Fits through a gap the width of a dime
Grayish-brown, much smaller than either rat species

look_alikes.difference: House mice are much smaller with rice-grain droppings; Norway rats are large with thick, capsule-shaped droppings and a burrow at ground level.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the droppings' size and shape.

copy.what_it_means: A mouse nibbles at 20-30 food sites a night rather than eating one big meal, which is why droppings show up in many places at once. One mouse is rarely just one — sealing dime-sized gaps helps keep the next one from using the same door.
copy.fact: A mouse nibbles at 20-30 food sites a night rather than one big meal, which is why droppings show up everywhere at once.
copy.blurb: One mouse is rarely one mouse. Sealing dime-sized gaps helps keep the next one from using the same door.

traits: Medium-large rat, 8 to 13 inches long including tail, with coarse, bristly grayish-brown fur
Short tail, often shorter than the body, sparsely haired and frequently looking stubbed or broken
Found in overgrown grassy lots, ditches, canal banks and weedy fields, not usually inside a tightly sealed home
Builds shallow surface runways through matted grass rather than the deep burrows or wall-void nests of house rodents

look_alikes.difference: Cotton rat has coarse fur and a short stubby tail, lives outdoors in grassy lots; roof rat has smooth fur, a tail longer than its body, prefers structures
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the tail length compared to the body and the fur texture.

safety_line: A Florida-specific hantavirus strain has been linked to this species; avoid stirring up dust from droppings or nests, and see a doctor if flu-like symptoms follow an exposure or cleanup.

copy.what_it_means: This is a native rat of overgrown, grassy areas rather than a typical house rodent, but it can move into sheds, garages or dense yard vegetation right next to a home. An inspection helps confirm what's actually present and where it's getting in or nesting before any exclusion work.
copy.fact: A hantavirus strain first identified near Miami in the 1990s was traced specifically to this species, a reminder that rodent droppings and nests are always worth handling carefully.

tech_notes: Confirm coarse pelage and short stubbed tail vs Rattus/Mus; habitat is typically overgrown grass/weeds near structures rather than wall voids. Note regional Black Creek Canal hantavirus association when advising on dropping/nest cleanup precautions (wet down before removal, gloves, ventilation).

review.notes: Both items resolved this session. Hantavirus risk: the Florida Department of Health's own hantavirus page confirms the virus "has been identified in cotton rats in Florida" and that most US cases are western, with only occasional eastern cases; multiple news reports citing CDC/FDOH figures put confirmed human hantavirus cases in Florida at about three total between 1993 and 2023 (including the original 1993 Dade County case that led to Black Creek Canal virus's discovery, PubMed 7623004) -- confirming this entry's 'rare' framing and calibrated (not overstated) safety_line/urgency. Peak months: the USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS) species report states hispid cotton rat populations "usually exhibit a bimodal breeding season, with peak litter production occurring in late spring and in late summer-early fall," which matches this entry's peak_months (Apr-Jun and Sep-Oct) closely; it's a general/federal rather than Florida-specific source, but settles the qualitative bimodal-peak claim. Per audit item 38: safety.structural changed from true to false since this entry makes no structural-damage claim anywhere -- it lives in grassy runways outdoors, not wall voids or wood. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Small, dark brown to black pellets, shaped like grains of rice (mice) or large grains of dark rice or olive pits (rats)
Found clustered along walls, in corners, cabinets, pantries, or attic insulation, often along a repeated travel path
Fresh droppings look moist, dark and shiny; old droppings turn dry, gray, and crumble easily
Often paired with a stale, musky odor in an enclosed space like a cabinet or attic

look_alikes.difference: Rodent droppings are solid, rice/olive-pit pellets in a scatter; roach droppings look like tiny pepper grains, often in a tighter pile
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the size and shape of the individual pieces.

safety_line: Droppings can carry germs and, rarely, viruses; avoid sweeping or vacuuming them dry, and see a doctor if flu-like symptoms follow a cleanup or heavy exposure.

copy.what_it_means: Fresh-looking droppings are evidence of recent rodent activity, but a photo cannot show whether that activity is ongoing. An inspection helps pin down which rodent left them and how it may be getting in before any cleanup or exclusion.
copy.fact: The age of a dropping is a real clue: fresh ones stay soft and dark for only a few days before drying out and turning gray.

tech_notes: Wet droppings with disinfectant before cleanup rather than dry sweeping/vacuuming to limit dust; identify species from pellet size/shape and location pattern to guide exclusion and trap placement.

traits: Fresh, light-colored gouges in wood or plastic with parallel groove marks from front teeth, often at corners or edges
Found on baseboards, door corners, wire insulation, stored boxes, or plastic pipe
Gnawed holes into a structure are usually rough-edged and about the size of a quarter or larger
Chewed spots darken and look greasy over time from repeated rubbing by the animal's fur

look_alikes.difference: Rodent gnaw marks are wide, rough gouges with visible parallel tooth grooves; powderpost beetle damage is tiny round pinholes with fine powder and no gouging
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the damaged area, checking for a wide gouge with grooves versus tiny round pinholes.

safety_line: Chewed electrical wiring is a fire risk; treat any chewed wire as worth an electrician's look alongside pest exclusion.

copy.what_it_means: Rodents gnaw constantly to keep their front teeth worn down, and they'll go through wood, plastic, and even wiring to do it. Fresh gouges anywhere in the home, especially near wiring, are worth an inspection before the damage or fire risk grows.
copy.fact: A rodent's front teeth never stop growing, which is exactly why it has to keep gnawing on something hard its whole life.

tech_notes: Distinguish fresh (light, clean-edged) from old (dark, worn) gnawing to gauge current activity; flag any chewed wiring for electrical follow-up separate from exclusion work.

Fresh gnawing in wood is usually light-colored with sharp, splintery edges. Old gnawing is smooth and darker" — matching this entry's traits almost verbatim (light/fresh vs. darker/older gouges, wire and structural gnawing, fire-risk framing). traits: Dark, greasy smudges along the same spot on a wall, baseboard, beam, or pipe where an animal squeezes through repeatedly
Found low along walls, at wall-floor junctions, or around consistent gaps like pipe penetrations
Marks build up gradually and darken with repeated contact over days to weeks
Often found alongside droppings or a worn, smoothed-down travel path in dust or insulation

look_alikes.difference: Rub marks are just a dark smudge with no material removed; gnaw marks show actual chewed-away wood, plastic or wire with tooth grooves
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the spot to see if material is missing (gnawing) or it's just a stain (rub mark).

copy.what_it_means: This greasy smudge marks a spot a rodent uses again and again to get from one place to another, which makes it one of the best clues for finding the actual entry point. It's worth pointing out during an inspection rather than just wiping away.
copy.fact: The mark comes from natural oils in the animal's fur, built up bit by bit from squeezing through the exact same gap night after night.

tech_notes: Use rub mark location to help pinpoint the active entry gap for exclusion; combine with droppings/gnaw evidence to confirm current activity level.
